insights.headline: You convert every loss into a purpose-statement within one or two lines, which lets you skip feeling the loss at all.
insights.explanation: Across all five stories, the instant something painful surfaces you reframe it as necessary before sitting in it: the house, dropping out, Mike's fraud exit, the breakup, this year's missed goal. The pattern is the timing, not the content — the reframe consistently lands within a line or two of the loss being named, which is what turns it from reflection into avoidance.

insights.headline: You fix people personally and directly, but never turn the fix into a claim on the system that failed them.
insights.explanation: You unwind Mrs. Delgado's fraud case over eleven weeks and forty calls without reporting it to corporate. You autopay your brother's rehab without visiting, and keep driving out to a customer whose equipment doesn't need you. In each case the fix is hands-on and bounded to the one person in front of you, never routed through escalation or a shared ask.

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Leadership and collaboration — when one of your nine guys has a compliance or performance problem, you'll handle it one-on-one and quietly rather than changing team process or escalating to the dealer.

insights.headline: You give sustained, unhurried presence to people who can't need anything ongoing from you, at a rate you don't give to people whose need is ongoing and entangling.
insights.explanation: You gave a full afternoon-to-dark to an 81-year-old stranger, changed her AC filter unprompted, unwound her fraud case for free over eleven weeks. You still visit a 91-year-old customer whose system needs nothing. You show up weekly for your grandmother even when she doesn't recognize you. Yet you haven't visited your brother in rehab despite Sundays already being spoken for by your grandmother, and you chose Cabo over being physically present while Kayla's father was dying, covering the gap with logistics and money instead.

insights.headline: You need a mentor with a quotable line to authorize your behavior, then keep the line running long after the person is gone from the story.

facts.what_happened: Speaker's first full solar sales year was 2021, working for an unnamed dealer under a manager referred to as Big Mike.
Speaker's earnings went from $12,000 in first quarter to $198,000 for the year.
Speaker was 24 years old at the time.
Events took place in Arizona.
Mike required team members to knock on a hundred doors before eating.
Speaker's daily door-knock count averaged 94-110 that summer; logged each count in the Notes app; notes still exist.
Documents ('docs') began appearing that raised concern.
DocuSigns were returned clean and fast on deals speaker believed customers hadn't actually completed; a teammate named Jarrett had elderly ('grandma-type') customers closing deals at 10pm.
The situation 'got handled eventually'; Mike is no longer in the industry.
A woman named Mrs. Delgado, age 81, living in Maryvale off Indian School, called the office and was eventually connected to speaker's cell number.

Mrs. Delgado's bill increased instead of decreasing; her solar system was undersized for her usage; there was a lien on her title she didn't understand; her signature appeared on documents she said she had not signed.
Speaker drove to her house and stayed from approximately 2pm until after dark.
Mrs. Delgado showed speaker photos of her late husband, who worked as a machinist, reportedly at Reynolds, and gave speaker a grocery bag of lemons.
Speaker noticed her AC filter was dirty/gray, bought a four-pack of filters at an Ace hardware store on 43rd, changed the filter, and moved her box fan from the front room to the bedroom.
It took eleven weeks and approximately forty phone calls for speaker to get Mrs. Delgado's situation resolved at no cost to her.
Speaker did not report the issue to corporate officially; resolved only Mrs. Delgado's individual case.
Mrs. Delgado died, speaker believes in 2023.
Her daughter texted speaker.
